Both final menu.js files add the document listeners when the menu opens, remove the same function references when it closes, and ignore taps inside the panel or on the toggle. The first agent also deals with focus, as the request asked: Escape moves focus back to the toggle and only acts when the menu is open. Its tests check that focus return and run a realistic open, tap inside, tap outside sequence. The second agent has no focus handling. It does add a useful test for tapping the toggle again to close, but its inside and outside tests open the menu with menu.open() instead of the button. On balance the first covers more of the request.

Both have the same core menu.js logic: document-level click and keydown listeners are added on open and removed on close, using stable function references, and the outside-tap handler ignores taps on the panel and button. The second agent also returns focus to the menu button after Escape, which the request asked for and is standard accessibility practice. Its Escape test fires on an element and lets the test helper pass it up to the document, so it checks the propagation path. It also checks taps inside and outside in one realistic sequence. Its downsides: it dropped the test that a second tap on the button closes the menu, its replacement test for the opening tap is trivial, and its added isOpen check is redundant. The first agent's tests cover more cases but fire Escape directly on the document and do nothing about focus. The focus handling slightly favours the second agent.

Both agents ended with working outside-tap and Escape closing. I couldn't verify either root-cause analysis because the original code wasn't visible. Agent 1 listens on the document in the capture phase, so a handler that stops an event from reaching the document can't block outside detection. It also returns focus to the menu button on Escape. Its tests cover listener cleanup after closing and focus return. Agent 2 listens in the bubble phase, doesn't restore focus and has no cleanup test. Its Escape test fires the key on the document itself. Agent 2's tests do open the menu by tapping the button, which is slightly more realistic. Overall, Agent 1 better covers the propagation, cleanup and focus checks the user asked for.

Both versions should close the menu on an outside tap or Escape and keep it open for taps inside. The second agent covers more of the request. Its capture-phase document listeners still fire if another handler stops the event from bubbling, and they are removed with matching arguments. It returns focus to the menu button on Escape, which the request mentioned. It also added tests that fire Escape on an element (not the document) and confirm the listeners are removed after closing. The first agent's code has normal bubbling listeners, does nothing about focus, has no cleanup test, and its Escape test fires only on the document. Neither agent's tests show the capture change is needed, and the original menu.js isn't shown, so confidence is medium.
